title: Randomized Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis
formal:
Is the following randomized Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis true?
\[
\forall\varepsilon\in(0,1)\ \exists k\in\mathbb N,\ k\ge3:
\quad\text{there is no bounded-error randomized algorithm for }k\text{-SAT}
\text{ with time }O\!\left(2^{(1-\varepsilon)n}\operatorname{poly}(L)\right).
\]
Here \(n\) is the number of variables, \(L\) is the complete binary input length, and algorithms are uniform probabilistic multitape Turing machines with worst-case running time over both inputs and coin outcomes, as defined below.

More precisely, for each \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), some fixed width \(k\ge3\) must exclude every machine \(M\) and fixed integers \(C\ge1,d\ge0\) satisfying, for every valid \(k\)-CNF formula \(F\),
\[
\Pr_r[M(\operatorname{enc}(F);r)=\operatorname{SAT}(F)]\ge\frac23,
\qquad
\forall r:\quad
t_M(\operatorname{enc}(F);r)
\le C\,2^{(1-\varepsilon)n(F)}(L(F)+1)^d.
\]
The machine returns a decision bit. The width may depend on \(\varepsilon\), but is fixed before the machine and the input are quantified.

This card uses the standard bounded-error Turing-machine formulation explicitly named RSETH in the later primary source’s \(\mathrm{BPTIME}\) definition. The original 2018 survey states its hypothesis under a logarithmic-word RAM convention. The choice of the later formulation is explicit; equivalence to a literal logarithmic-address-space interpretation of that earlier RAM convention is not asserted.
why: This hypothesis is a central proposed barrier for randomized algorithms: it specifies whether exhaustive assignment search becomes essentially optimal as clause width increases. It supports fine-grained conditional lower bounds where randomized target algorithms must also be excluded, and links exact satisfiability complexity to tight complexity questions for other fundamental problems. A proof or refutation would change a major foundation of modern algorithmic hardness, well beyond the performance of one SAT solver.
status_note: The original survey explicitly states randomized SETH as a hypothesis in 2018, and the checked 2023 primary revision explicitly states the named RSETH in BPTIME, which is the formulation developed here. The original survey’s different word-RAM convention is disclosed rather than declared equivalent. Bounded primary-source checks through 16 September 2026 found no verified proof or refutation of this complete bounded-error Turing-machine hypothesis; the checked 2026 PPSZ preprint concerns fixed width three. This sourced-open status is not an exhaustive literature certificate or a completed Lean proof.

importance.reason: A defining hardness hypothesis for randomized exact exponential-time and fine-grained algorithms, with consequences for fundamental satisfiability, set-system and polynomial-time problems. Its significance lies in excluding a uniform positive saving across all fixed clause widths and in strengthening deterministic hardness to bounded-error algorithms. This individual assessment follows that mathematical breadth, not the age of the survey or the inherited unassessed midpoint.

sentences: Randomized SETH asks whether every fixed positive saving in the exhaustive-search exponent fails at some fixed clause width.
Inputs are arbitrary explicitly encoded \(k\)-CNF formulas, with the number of variables in the exponent and a polynomial factor in input length.
The developed formulation uses uniform fair-coin Turing machines, error at most \(1/3\) on every input, and worst-case time over random bits.
A refutation needs one positive exponent saving valid for every fixed width, although its algorithm and polynomial factor may depend on that width.
The standard BPTIME model is explicitly sourced separately from the survey’s RAM convention, and recent fixed-width SAT improvements do not settle the hypothesis.

definitions:
Fix an integer \(k\ge3\). A \(k\)-CNF formula \(F\) is a finite list of clauses, each a finite list of at most \(k\) literals. A literal is a variable \(x_i\) or its negation \(\neg x_i\). The distinct variables occurring in the entire formula are exactly \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), so \(n\) counts variables, not clauses or encoding bits. Repeated literals, repeated clauses and clauses containing both signs of a variable are allowed. A Boolean assignment is a map \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\to\{0,1\}\); it satisfies \(F\) when every clause has at least one true literal. The empty clause is false, the empty conjunction is true, and the empty conjunction has \(n=0\). Define \(\operatorname{SAT}(F)=1\) if some assignment satisfies \(F\), and \(0\) otherwise.

Use the following explicit binary encoding. For each integer \(a\ge0\), let \(\operatorname{bin}(a+1)\) be the binary expansion of \(a+1\) with no leading zeros, let \(b\) be its length, and put \(\operatorname{code}(a)=1^b0\operatorname{bin}(a+1)\). Encode the number \(n\) of variables and the number \(m\) of clauses using this code. Then encode each clause by its coded length, followed by its literals in their listed order. Encode a literal by one sign bit, \(0\) for positive and \(1\) for negated, followed by \(\operatorname{code}(i)\) for its variable index. Require \(1\le i\le n\), all declared lists to be fully present, every declared variable to occur, no trailing bits, and every clause length to be at most \(k\). Let \(L=|\operatorname{enc}(F)|\).

The inputs range over all such formulas. There is no promise of linearly many clauses, bounded variable occurrences, a unique satisfying assignment, a gap in the optimum number of satisfied clauses, or a random input distribution. The clause width is a fixed constant for each language \(k\)-SAT; it does not grow with the input length. The model allows arbitrarily many explicitly listed clauses, including duplicates, and the displayed polynomial factor in \(L\) includes their processing.

A machine has one finite program, finitely many tapes and finite tape alphabets, with these choices fixed independently of input length. Its tapes have cells indexed by the nonnegative integers, all heads start at cell zero, and an attempted left move from cell zero leaves that head there. The read-only input tape contains the encoding starting in cell zero, followed by an end marker and blanks; work tapes are initially blank. The finite control starts in a fixed initial state and has halting states labelled by the decision bits \(0\) and \(1\). At each transition the machine reads or writes only the symbols under its heads and moves each head by at most one cell. It may request one fresh fair random bit during a transition. The random source \(r\) is an infinite sequence of independent unbiased bits; a run reads a finite prefix before halting. All transitions, including input access, random-bit generation and internal computation, count toward \(t_M\). There is no unit-cost random access, unbounded-integer arithmetic, quantum operation, oracle or advice depending on input length.

A \(k\)-SAT algorithm in the quantified class halts with output \(0\) or \(1\) on every input and every random sequence. It rejects malformed encodings in polynomial time in their bit length, with a fixed polynomial for that machine. On each valid formula its answer is correct with probability at least \(2/3\), independently of whether the formula is satisfiable. Thus errors on both yes-instances and no-instances are permitted. The runtime bound is required for every random sequence, not only in expectation or with high probability. There is no additional space bound.

The constants \(C,d\) and the program may depend on the fixed width \(k\) and on a proposed saving \(\varepsilon\), but cannot depend on \(F\), \(n\), \(L\) or the realized random bits. Any finite exceptional set of input lengths can be covered by increasing \(C\). Every algorithm is uniform across input lengths. A different algorithm may be considered for each width; no computable procedure selecting those algorithms from \(k\) is built into the hypothesis.

The quantifier over \(\varepsilon\) asks about every fixed positive saving in the exponent. It does not assert a \(2^{n-o(n)}\) lower bound for a single fixed width, and it does not preclude a width-dependent saving tending to zero as \(k\) increases. The claim also does not replace bounded-width satisfiability by arbitrary-width CNF-SAT. The randomness belongs to the algorithm while correctness and time are worst-case over formulas.
answer_criterion:
Provide a complete, mathematically correct Lean proof of the displayed hypothesis or of its full negation in the stated machine and input model.

A positive answer must establish that, for every real \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), some fixed integer \(k\ge3\) excludes all machines and constants satisfying both the correctness and runtime conditions. It must cover all uniform bounded-error randomized algorithms, not only a selected algorithm or a restricted family.

A negative answer must establish the quantifier order
\[
\exists\varepsilon_0\in(0,1)\ \forall k\ge3\
\exists M_k,\ C_k\ge1,\ d_k\ge0\
\forall F\in k\text{-CNF}:
\]
\[
\Pr_r[M_k(\operatorname{enc}(F);r)=\operatorname{SAT}(F)]\ge\frac23
\quad\text{and}\quad
\forall r:\ 
t_{M_k}(\operatorname{enc}(F);r)
\le C_k\,2^{(1-\varepsilon_0)n(F)}(L(F)+1)^{d_k}.
\]
Here \(C_k,d_k\) are integers and each \(M_k\) meets all machine, termination and malformed-input requirements above. The same positive \(\varepsilon_0\) must work for every fixed width; programs and polynomial factors may vary with the width. Proving these existential witnesses for every width suffices without an additional requirement of one algorithm that accepts the width as input.

An improvement only for one width, a saving that vanishes as the width grows, average-case performance, or a result under an additional unproved hypothesis does not settle this statement. A proof only about deterministic algorithms establishes a different claim unless it also yields the required randomized statement. Numerical evidence about running-time bases and a Lean definition of the hypothesis alone are insufficient.

context_blocks.text: The 2018 survey explicitly extends the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis to randomized algorithms in Hypothesis 1. The later definition by Ron-Zewi and Rothblum names the hypothesis RSETH and states it using bounded-error probabilistic time. This card adopts that standard Turing-machine formulation and records the original survey’s different global RAM convention rather than silently identifying the two models.

Exhaustive search examines \(2^n\) assignments. For any particular fixed clause width, randomized algorithms can improve its exponential base. The hypothesis concerns whether the savings can be kept bounded away from zero across every fixed width, so improvements for \(3\)-SAT are compatible with it.

Cygan and coauthors formulate the randomized growth rate with error probability at most \(1/3\) and a polynomial factor in the complete input size. They distinguish the hypothesis for all fixed widths from the weaker assertion that unrestricted-width CNF-SAT has no fixed improvement over exhaustive search. Their work also connects the bounded-width hypothesis to corresponding exponential-time barriers for Hitting Set, Set Splitting and Not-All-Equal SAT.

The randomized claim excludes a larger class of algorithms than deterministic SETH in the same bit model, so it implies that deterministic hypothesis. Randomized ETH asks instead for a positive exponential-time barrier already for \(3\)-SAT; it does not demand that the optimal exponent approach one with increasing width. Nondeterministic SETH, parity hypotheses and assumptions about randomly sampled formulas concern other algorithmic or input models.

The July 2026 preprint on PPSZ reports improved randomized bounds for Unique-\(3\)-SAT and general \(3\)-SAT. Its theorems address that fixed width and do not supply the common positive exponent saving for every width that would negate rSETH. This bounded literature check records the preprint’s scope without treating it as a verified resolution of the hypothesis.

checked_sources: Read the complete active TCS-6935 and docs/RULES.md. Read active related TCS-6593 (deterministic ETH), TCS-6595 (deterministic SETH), TCS-0562 (nondeterministic SETH) and TCS-7313 (deterministic ETH versus sparse Gap-ETH). None has the same algorithm-class and quantifier target as this randomized hypothesis. In the shared Turing model, rSETH implies deterministic SETH because deterministic machines are a subclass; the converse is not asserted. Do not merge these distinct significant variants automatically.

Downloaded the actual current author PDF eccentri.pdf under rseth-survey2018. Read the introduction, Section 2.1, Hypothesis 1, and following distinctions. Hypothesis 1 is on PDF p. 4, with every epsilon, some k at least 3, width at most k, n variables, and randomized algorithms. There is no sparse-formula promise. Its global model on the same page is O(log N)-bit word-RAM, N the input length; neither an error constant nor an all-coins/expectation convention is written into Hypothesis 1.

Consequential model issue disclosed early to the parent: under a literal single-word address convention, O(log L)-bit RAMs address only polynomially many words, while unrestricted exponential-time multitape machines may use exponentially much space. Polynomial simulation alone does not preserve a saving below the base-two exhaustive-search exponent, so no equivalence was silently claimed. The parent approved adopting the later explicitly named BPTIME rSETH formulation as a supported editorial model choice; the public formal statement discloses the distinction.

Downloaded and read Ron-Zewi–Rothblum ECCC TR19-127 revision 2, title page dated 30 September 2023; ECCC records revision posting on 3 November 2023. Appendix A Definition A.1, printed/PDF p. 44, explicitly names RSETH and uses k-SAT not in BPTIME(2^{(1-epsilon)n}). This is the primary basis for unrestricted uniform bounded-error probabilistic Turing time. The card unpacks the usual finite-program, finite-alphabet, finite-tape fair-coin convention; it imposes no additional space bound.

Downloaded actual arXiv:1112.2275v3 (27 March 2014, PDF dated 28 March). Printed p. 1/PDF p. 2 explicitly allows bounded-error randomized algorithms; Section 2.2.1 printed p. 6/PDF p. 7 distinguishes bounded width from a separate linear-density promise. Definition 2.1 printed p. 8/PDF p. 9 defines the randomized exponent with error probability at most 1/3 and factor polynomial in total input size, then states the limiting-exponent SETH. The following paragraph explicitly warns that its failure need not give a fixed-saving algorithm for unrestricted-width CNF-SAT. Preserve the per-width existential algorithm quantifier; do not add one effective algorithm generator for all k.

Polynomial input-factor normalization is substantive and sourced, rather than permitting a vacuous input-reading lower bound on arbitrarily padded formulas. For a fixed width k, removing repeated literals, tautological clauses and duplicate clauses yields at most sum_{j=0}^k 2^j binomial(n,j) distinct non-tautological clauses. The resulting length is polynomial in n for fixed k. Preprocessing arbitrary explicit input costs poly(L); the polynomial length factors on reduced instances can be absorbed by any fixed smaller exponent saving. Thus the full every-epsilon assertion uses the customary polynomial-input-factor normalization without a hidden linear-clause promise. The audit does not assert pointwise equality of exact runtime bounds at a fixed epsilon.

The chosen bounded-error constant is directly supported by Cygan et al. Definition 2.1. The statement permits both false positives and false negatives. For this satisfiability hypothesis the conventional one-sided and two-sided exclusion formulations can also be related with polynomial overhead: amplify a decider to inverse-polynomial error, make at most n adaptive restricted-formula queries to recover a candidate assignment, then verify it. Width does not increase and the number of actual variables does not increase; verification eliminates false positives. This explanatory normalization remains in the audit, not as a public solution hint.

Worst-case time over all fair-coin runs is the BPTIME convention. An expected-time bounded-error speedup with a uniform bound on each input can be amplified by constant repetitions and truncated at a constant multiple of its expected-time bound; the added error can be kept below 1/3. If necessary, choose a smaller rational exponent saving to make the cutoff explicit. Conversely worst-case bounds imply expected bounds. This justifies treating the overall hypothesis as robust to the usual expected-time convention after changing constants or slightly shrinking the saving, not equating every individual machine guarantee. No conversion from arbitrary real/quantum randomness is asserted.

The negation is some one positive epsilon_0 followed by every fixed width and then an algorithm and constants for that width. The program need not be the same for different widths, but is finite and uniform in input size for each width. A particular small-width speedup, a width-dependent saving tending to zero, or a mere sparse/random/unique-input result cannot refute this quantified statement. Positive lower-bound proofs must also address two-sided randomized machines. No conjectural premise is built into either answer.

Bounded later searches through 16 September 2026 checked exact randomized-strong-ETH/BPTIME formulations, recent k-SAT/PPSZ work and apparent SETH-refutation titles. Downloaded arXiv:2607.10697v1 and read pp. 1–3, Theorem 1.1 and Corollary 1.2. Its claimed numerical improvement is exclusively for Unique-3-SAT and general 3-SAT. The preprint is not promoted to an independently verified best-known theorem; the card uses only its checked scope. No verified proof or refutation of the full rSETH statement was recovered in this bounded check.

Checked primary abstract and metadata of Kulikov–Mihajlin, If Edge Coloring is Hard under SETH, then SETH is False, arXiv:2607.21276v1 (23 July 2026; notes the SOSA 2024 publication). It is a conditional barrier to certain edge-coloring hardness reductions, not an unconditional SAT speedup or proof that SETH is false. It is not needed in the public card. Average-case random-k-SAT and stronger quantitative SSETH leads were kept distinct from worst-case randomized SETH.
